questions.explanation: ESXi Shell and SSH give root-level access to the hypervisor itself — not just a guest. An attacker with ESXi root access can power off, clone, or exfiltrate all VMs, access VM disks directly, capture VM memory (including running credentials), and pivot to the management network.

questions.question: macOS Gatekeeper prevents unsigned applications from running. What is the standard technique to bypass Gatekeeper when distributing a malicious application?

options.A: Exploit a kernel vulnerability to disable Gatekeeper system-wide
options.B: Obtain an Apple developer certificate (free or paid), sign the application, optionally notarise it with Apple — or socially engineer the user into right-click > Open to bypass the quarantine check
options.C: Modify the /etc/gatekeeper.conf file to add an exception
options.D: Install a malicious kernel extension to disable code signing checks

questions.explanation: The most practical bypass for most attacks is obtaining a legitimate (or stolen) Apple developer certificate to sign the payload, or tricking users into using right-click > Open which bypasses the Gatekeeper block. The quarantine attribute (com.apple.quarantine) applied to downloaded files triggers Gatekeeper; files received through non-browser methods (AirDrop, etc.) may not get this attribute.

questions.question: What is Transparency, Consent and Control (TCC) on macOS and how do attackers attempt to bypass it?

options.A: TCC is Apple's App Store review process; attackers submit malicious apps that pass review
options.B: TCC is a macOS privacy framework requiring user consent before apps can access Camera, Microphone, Contacts, Location, and full disk. Attackers bypass it by injecting into TCC-approved processes (e.g., Finder, Terminal) or exploiting vulnerabilities that reset TCC databases
options.C: TCC is the macOS firewall component; attackers bypass it with kernel exploits
options.D: TCC controls code signing; attackers bypass it by stripping the code signature from binaries

questions.explanation: TCC enforces user-consent gates on sensitive resources. A common bypass is to inject code into a process that already has TCC permissions (e.g., inject into Terminal which has full disk access). Historical TCC bypasses include direct database manipulation (before SIP protected it) and exploiting migration tools.

questions.question: What does System Integrity Protection (SIP) on macOS protect, and what are the limits of this protection?

options.A: SIP encrypts all user data on the system volume; it does not protect system binaries
options.B: SIP prevents modification of core OS directories (/System, /usr, /bin, /sbin) and system processes even by root; however, it does not protect user directories, third-party software, or network traffic
options.C: SIP is a firewall that prevents unauthorised inbound connections to system services
options.D: SIP prevents applications from running without a valid Apple notarisation ticket

questions.explanation: SIP (rootless mode) restricts even root from modifying protected OS paths, loading unsigned kernel extensions, or attaching to system processes with a debugger. It does not protect user home directories, /Applications (third-party), or application data — so malware can still persist in LaunchAgents and user directories.

questions.question: An attacker wants to persist on a compromised macOS system without root. Which persistence mechanism is available to standard user accounts?

options.A: Installing a LaunchDaemon in /Library/LaunchDaemons/ (requires root)
options.B: Adding a LaunchAgent plist to ~/Library/LaunchAgents/ — this runs automatically at login for the user without requiring any elevated privileges
options.C: Modifying /etc/rc.common (requires root)
options.D: Installing a kernel extension in /Library/Extensions/ (requires root and SIP bypass)

questions.explanation: ~/Library/LaunchAgents/ is writable by the user and any plist placed there is executed by launchd at login. It is the standard user-level persistence location for macOS malware, analogous to HKCU\Run in Windows. LaunchDaemons require root and run as root at boot.

questions.question: What is the macOS Keychain and what attack technique targets it during a post-exploitation engagement?

options.A: Keychain is the macOS update mechanism; attackers manipulate it to prevent security updates
options.B: Keychain is the macOS credential store for passwords, certificates, and private keys. Post-exploitation, attackers use security dump-keychain or tools like Chainbreaker to extract stored credentials — the user's login password often unlocks the login keychain
options.C: Keychain is the macOS firewall rule database; attackers modify it to allow reverse shells
options.D: Keychain stores FileVault encryption keys; attackers extract it to decrypt the disk offline

questions.explanation: The macOS Keychain stores Wi-Fi passwords, website credentials, certificates, and application secrets. Tools like `security dump-keychain -d` (when run in the user's session context) or Chainbreaker can extract credentials. Many keychain items are unlocked when the user logs in, making post-exploitation keychain dumping very productive.

questions.question: What is 'tailgating' (also called 'piggybacking') and what is the most effective control to prevent it?

options.A: Following a target vehicle into a secured car park; prevented by ANPR (Automatic Number Plate Recognition)
options.B: Following an authorised person through a secured door without presenting credentials yourself; best prevented by mantrap/airlock entry systems with single-person detection (one person per authentication)
options.C: Intercepting wireless credentials by following an employee home; prevented by WPA3 Enterprise
options.D: Cloning an RFID badge by walking close to someone; prevented by Faraday badge sleeves

questions.explanation: Tailgating exploits social conventions (holding a door open) to bypass physical access controls. Mantrap/airlock doors — where only one person can enter per badge swipe — are the most effective technical control. Staff training to challenge tailgaters also helps but relies on human compliance.

questions.question: An attacker successfully reads an employee's HID Prox Card from 30cm away using a commercially available reader. What class of attack is this and how is it mitigated?

options.A: A relay attack; mitigated by distance-bounding protocols
options.B: An RFID skimming attack against low-frequency (125kHz) proximity cards which transmit credentials without encryption; mitigated by upgrading to MIFARE DESFire or similar high-frequency encrypted smart cards (13.56MHz) and using Faraday shielding sleeves
options.C: A brute-force attack against the card's PIN; mitigated by increasing PIN complexity
options.D: A man-in-the-middle attack; mitigated by certificate pinning on the card reader

questions.explanation: HID Prox and EM4100 proximity cards broadcast their card number in cleartext with no authentication or encryption. Tools like the Proxmark can read and clone these cards from short distances. The mitigation is replacing them with cryptographically authenticated smart cards (MIFARE DESFire EV2/EV3, iCLASS Seos).

questions.question: What is a 'rubber ducky' style attack in the context of physical security testing?

options.A: Using a squeaky toy to distract security guards
options.B: Inserting a device (USB Rubber Ducky, Bash Bunny) that masquerades as a USB keyboard and automatically types a pre-programmed payload at high speed when plugged in, bypassing application whitelisting that only blocks executables
options.C: Planting a Wi-Fi pineapple in a rubber duck decoy to conduct wireless attacks
options.D: A social engineering technique where an attacker pretends to be a helpless visitor to gain entry

questions.explanation: HID-emulation attacks (USB Rubber Ducky, Bash Bunny in HID mode) present as a standard keyboard. The OS trusts keyboard input implicitly, so the device types commands at superhuman speed (opening PowerShell, running a payload) in seconds. Mitigations include USB device management policies, port blocking, and disabling AutoRun/AutoPlay.

questions.question: During a physical penetration test, a tester photographs the underside of keyboards and the area under monitors. What are they looking for?

options.A: Evidence of USB keyloggers attached between the keyboard cable and the PC
options.B: Passwords written on sticky notes — a common finding that can give immediate access to systems without any technical attack
options.C: MAC addresses written on equipment labels
options.D: Asset tags for inventory enumeration

questions.explanation: Written credentials are one of the most common findings in physical security assessments. Employees write passwords on sticky notes attached to monitors, keyboards, or stored in unlocked drawers. These immediately compromise accounts without any technical exploitation. The finding demonstrates that password complexity requirements drive users toward insecure storage.

questions.question: What is 'lock picking' in the context of a physical penetration test and what is its legal and ethical requirement before conducting it?

options.A: Lock picking is illegal in all jurisdictions and should never be included in a penetration test
options.B: Lock picking involves manipulating lock mechanisms (using picks, tension wrenches, bump keys, or bypass tools) to open locked doors without the key. It requires explicit written authorisation covering the specific locks and locations to be tested, before any attempt is made
options.C: Lock picking refers to social engineering a locksmith to grant access, requiring no special authorisation
options.D: Lock picking is only legal if conducted by a licensed locksmith and so the penetration tester must hold a locksmith qualification

questions.explanation: Physical penetration testing techniques including lock picking require explicit, written authorisation that clearly defines scope (which buildings, which locks, what hours). Without this, the activity constitutes criminal damage or breaking and entering. Legal requirements vary by jurisdiction — some countries restrict lock-pick tool possession itself.

questions.question: What security risk arises from running a Docker container with the --privileged flag?

options.A: The container can only be accessed by root on the host
options.B: The --privileged flag disables all Linux namespace and capability isolation, giving the container full access to host devices and kernel features — effectively the same as root on the host, enabling a trivial container escape
options.C: The container is restricted to using 100% of one CPU core
options.D: The --privileged flag exposes container ports directly to the internet

questions.explanation: A privileged container has access to all host devices (/dev), can load kernel modules, and has every Linux capability enabled. Escape is trivial: mount the host filesystem via /dev/sda, write a cron job or SSH key, and exit the container. Containers should run with minimal capabilities (--cap-drop ALL, --cap-add only what is needed).

questions.question: An attacker compromises a container and finds that the Docker socket (/var/run/docker.sock) is mounted inside it. How can this be exploited?

options.A: The attacker can only stop and restart containers, not escape to the host
options.B: The Docker socket gives the container control of the Docker daemon on the host. The attacker runs a new privileged container mounting the host filesystem, chroots into it, and achieves full host root access — a complete container escape
options.C: Mounting the Docker socket allows the container to pull images from Docker Hub only
options.D: The attacker can read other container logs but cannot modify the host

questions.explanation: Mounting the Docker socket inside a container is equivalent to giving it root on the host. The container can issue Docker API commands to start new privileged containers, mount /host-root into them, then chroot out of the container to interact with the full host OS. This is a common misconfiguration in CI/CD pipelines and monitoring agents.

questions.question: What is a 'distroless' container image and what security benefit does it provide?

options.A: A container image with no operating system at all, used only for data storage
options.B: A minimal container image containing only the application and its runtime dependencies — no shell, package manager, or debug tools. This significantly reduces the attack surface because attackers cannot use common post-exploitation tools even if they achieve code execution
options.C: A container image that automatically removes itself after the container stops
options.D: A container image built without any Linux distribution branding, indistinguishable from other distributions

questions.explanation: Distroless images (popularised by Google) omit shells (/bin/sh), package managers (apt, apk), and other OS utilities. Post-exploitation activities that rely on bash, curl, wget, or package installation are blocked. Combined with read-only filesystems and no-new-privileges flags, distroless images significantly harden container deployments.

questions.question: What is a 'software supply chain attack' and which high-profile incident demonstrated its risk?

options.A: An attack on the physical logistics chain delivering hardware components; demonstrated by the Bloomberg Supermicro hardware implant claims
options.B: Compromising a software vendor, build system, or dependency so that malicious code is distributed to downstream users through a trusted update mechanism; demonstrated by the SolarWinds Orion compromise (SUNBURST backdoor, 2020)
options.C: Exploiting weak supplier contracts to access customer data; demonstrated by the Target HVAC vendor breach
options.D: Attacking the software escrow service holding source code for critical infrastructure

questions.explanation: In the SolarWinds attack, threat actors compromised the build pipeline and injected the SUNBURST backdoor into legitimate Orion software updates, signed with SolarWinds' own certificate. 18,000 organisations installed the trojanised update. This exemplifies supply chain attacks: the distribution mechanism itself is weaponised.

questions.question: What is the purpose of SAST (Static Application Security Testing) and at which stage of the SDLC should it be applied?

options.A: SAST analyses running applications by sending malicious inputs; applied in production during staging
options.B: SAST analyses source code or compiled bytecode without executing it, detecting vulnerabilities (SQL injection patterns, hardcoded secrets, unsafe functions) at development or CI/CD pipeline stage — 'shift left' before code reaches production
options.C: SAST tests the application's security headers by making HTTP requests; applied pre-release
options.D: SAST monitors production application logs for attack patterns; applied continuously in production

questions.explanation: SAST is a 'white-box' technique that inspects source code, bytecode, or binary without executing it. It is most valuable when integrated into CI/CD pipelines so developers get security feedback on every commit — the 'shift left' security principle. Tools include Semgrep, SonarQube, Checkmarx, and Bandit (Python).

questions.question: A developer accidentally commits an AWS access key to a public GitHub repository. What should be the FIRST action taken, and why?

options.A: Use git rebase to remove the commit from history — this is sufficient because the commit is removed
options.B: Immediately revoke/rotate the AWS key in the AWS console — the key should be treated as fully compromised because automated scanners (GitGuardian, truffleHog bots) detect and harvest secrets from public commits within seconds of publication
options.C: Make the repository private immediately — this prevents any further exposure
options.D: Open a GitHub support ticket to have the commit removed from GitHub's servers

questions.explanation: Automated secret-harvesting bots scan public GitHub pushes in real time. Even if the commit is deleted or the repo made private within minutes, the secret must be assumed compromised and revoked immediately. Git history rewriting is secondary — the revocation/rotation is the critical first step.
